catalog_quote: Both Hindko and Panjabi have phonemic tone, albeit with differing systems, but Saraiki does not. ... The high tone, on the other hand, is relatively salient. ... In two-syllable words the high falling tone is always on the first syllable, and never on the second, as in [kóṛā] ‘leper’. ... For stress in Hindko we rely mainly on Bahri (1963), which, though it describes a Hindko variety different from that of Hazara, is considered by Shackle (1980: 487) “to be taken as typical of Hindko”. Bahri (1963: 141) focuses on the strong stress accent in Hindko varieties, and considers the widespread elision of vowels found in Hindko to be due to this strong stress accent. Varma (1936: 92) further states that in “Lahnda” there is only one primary word stress; secondary word stress is not found. sweep_summary: nort2662 Northern Hindko is in the catalog as 'undetermined' on Bashir & Conners 2019, whose stress section is second-hand (Bahri 1963, a different variety) and rule-less. The sweep list had one title-keyword item, Nawaz 2014 (PhD, IIU Islamabad, Tanawal/Hazara Hindko), already on file with a text layer; re-read in full: its 'selected suprasegmental features' are syllable structure and gemination only, and it explicitly defers stress and tone to future work (abstract p. xv, pp. 97-98, p. 305) -- silent on stress, priority none. The best first-hand statement actually read is Haroon-Ur-Rashid 2015 (PhD, UAJK; Hazara Hindko; also already on file): quantity-sensitive unbounded right-headed stress -- the superheavy (CVVC) syllable is stressed wherever it occurs, otherwise the penult with final-mora extrametricality (abstract p. iii; sec. 5.3.3 pp. 211-215; native-speaker experiment p. 217). It supersedes the catalog's deciding source for the stress coding (refines 'undetermined' to weight-sensitive rightmost-heavy-else-penult). No new files were fetched sources; written at (file -> citation -> URL for both theses and the irrelevant JoLaCE 2018 paper held from the earlier fetch).

new_statements.quote: "Hindko is a quantity-sensitive unbounded rhythmic right headed language. Stress is taken by the super heavy syllable irrespective of its occurrence in words, otherwise penultimate syllable is assigned stress. In case of a tie in terms of syllable weight, extrametricality comes to play." (abstract p. iii) ... "The rightmost heaviest syllable is assigned stress which may be bi-moraic or tri-moraic in a word." (p. 214) ... "Hindko native speakers stress the heaviest syllable in the word. In the event of tie, they prefer to stress the penult." (p. 217)

new_statements.reading: Weight-sensitive, unbounded, right-oriented lexical stress in monomorphemic Hazara Hindko words: a superheavy (CVVC, trimoraic) syllable takes stress wherever it stands (antepenult ˈkot̪ʰ.rɑ 'dirty', ˈkɑl.si.ri 'woman'; penult tʃɑ.ˈbut̪.rɑ; final ɦɑ.ˈɽik 'seed', sət̪.jɑ.ˈnɑs); when syllables tie in weight the final mora is extrametrical and the penult is stressed (ˈsom.vɑr 'Monday', ɦəd̪.ˈvɑ̃.nɑ̃ 'water-melon', ˈsɑ.vɑ 'green'). Author's typology (p. 189): 'rightmost heavy, else rightmost' with final extrametricality, i.e. rightmost-heavy else penult. A 10-speaker stress-marking experiment (p. 217, >=80% agreement per item) matches. This is a first-hand, Hazara-specific, corpus-plus-experiment description, whereas the catalog's deciding source (Bashir & Conners 2019, pp. 49-50) says 'For stress in Hindko we rely mainly on Bahri (1963), which... describes a Hindko variety different from that of Hazara' and gives no placement rule; the catalog's 'undetermined' coding should be refined to a weight-sensitive unbounded (rightmost superheavy, else penult) system on this source.

audit.recode_to: Quantity-sensitive, right-oriented unbounded ('rightmost heaviest') with penult default: three-way moraic weight (CV light; CVV/CVC heavy; CVVC/CVCC superheavy); stress the superheavy syllable wherever it is (antepenult/penult/final attested in trisyllables); otherwise, with final-mora extrametricality resolving ties, stress the penult; no secondary stress reported. Deciding source Haroon-Ur-Rashid 2015 sec. 5.3.3 pp. 211-216 and abstract p. iii; keep BC2019 pp. 49-50, 53, 72 for the stress-tone interaction (high tone only on stressed syllables) and the /ˈbaṭṭā/ ~ /baˈṭā-/ pair, which HR2015 Table 5.26 independently reproduces. Evidence grade should move from 'open-text, source defers' to 'dissertation with corpus + native-speaker experiment (non-instrumental for stress)'.

sources.citation: Nawaz, Muhammad. 2014. A Descriptive Study of Segmental and Selected Suprasegmental Features of Hindko Dialect Spoken in Tanawal, Hazara. PhD dissertation, Department of English, International Islamic University, Islamabad. 368 pp. (Glottolog 665847, hhtype phonology)
sources.quote: The 'selected suprasegmental features' are syllable structure, syllabic consonants, clusters and gemination only: 'It is suggested that remaining suprasegmental features of Hindko such as stress and tones should be investigated' (abstract); 'there is intense need to work on the remaining two suprasegmental features of Hindko, i.e. stress and tones' (conclusion). No stress-placement statement.
sources.note: Glottolog's only 'phonology' ref for nort2662; fetched sources now to close the list -- turns out to exclude stress and tone by design (silent), so it cannot change the coding but documents that no competing Hazara stress account exists there.
